subject: Surgery
summary: Soft‑tissue infections range from superficial cellulitis to necrotising fasciitis. Recognise severity, identify common tropical pathogens, and start targeted therapy even when diagnostics are limited.

sections.p: Infection of skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia or muscle caused by bacteria, fungi or parasites. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by limited labs when available.
b: Cellulitis: diffuse erythema, warmth, tenderness, no fluctuance.
Abscess: localized fluctuant collection.
Necrotising fasciitis: severe pain out of proportion, rapid spread, systemic toxicity.

sections.p: Use the Eron classification (or similar) to guide admission and antibiotics.
b: Stage I: mild, no systemic signs, treat outpatient.
Stage II: moderate, comorbidities or limited systemic signs, consider short admission.
Stage III: severe, systemic toxicity, extensive disease – admit, IV therapy.
Stage IV: life‑threatening, organ failure – ICU, surgical debridement.

sections.p: Pathogens differ by depth, geography and host factors.
b: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) – most common for cellulitis and abscess.
Streptococcus pyogenes – classic for cellulitis and necrotising fasciitis.
Gram‑negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella) – common in diabetic foot or perineal infections.
Anaerobes (Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus) – polymicrobial wounds, bite injuries.
Fungi (Candida, Sporothrix) – in immunocompromised or chronic ulcers.
Parasites (Leishmania) – endemic cutaneous lesions in East Africa.

sections.p: History focuses on portal of entry, trauma, animal bite, recent surgery, diabetes or HIV. Examination looks for depth, spread, systemic signs.
b: Rapidly expanding erythema, warmth, edema.
Pain out of proportion → suspect necrotising fasciitis.
Fluctuance → abscess.
Crepitus → gas‑forming organisms.
Systemic: fever, tachycardia, hypotension.

t.b: Is there systemic inflammation? ↑WBC or left shift supports severe infection.
How intense is the inflammatory response? Very high values suggest deep or necrotising infection.
Is bacteremia present? Positive cultures guide definitive therapy; if unavailable, treat empirically.
What organism is causing the infection? Gram stain and culture direct antibiotic choice; if lab missing, use broad‑spectrum coverage.
Is there a fluid collection? Detects abscesses or fascial thickening when clinical exam is equivocal.
Is there gas in soft tissue? Presence supports necrotising infection with gas‑forming organisms.

sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent surgical input or ICU care.
b: Pain disproportionate to skin findings.
Rapid progression of erythema (>2 cm per hour).
Crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis.
Sepsis: hypotension, tachypnea, altered mental status.
Underlying diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression.

sections.p: Start empiric antibiotics promptly, adjust for depth and local resistance, and consider surgery when indicated.
b: Empiric oral flucloxacillin or cloxacillin for MSSA cellulitis if no MRSA risk.
Add clindamycin or linezolid if MRSA suspected or severe toxin‑mediated disease.
For necrotising fasciitis: broad‑spectrum IV (e.g., carbapenem + clindamycin + vancomycin if MRSA likely).
Diabetic foot or polymicrobial wounds: ampicillin‑sulbactam or ceftriaxone + metronidazole.
Surgical drainage for abscesses; early debridement for necrotising fasciitis.
Supportive care: fluids, analgesia, glycaemic control, wound care.

sections.p: Monitor clinical response; arrange wound care and address risk factors.
b: Re‑evaluate after 48‑72 h – improvement should be evident.
Educate on foot hygiene, glycaemic control, wound dressing, and prompt care for bites.
Vaccinate against tetanus; consider decolonisation for recurrent MRSA.
Deep vein thrombosis – unilateral leg swelling without skin changes.
Cellulitis‑like erythema nodosum – tender nodules, no warmth.
Contact dermatitis – itching predominates, no systemic signs.
Vasculitis – purpura, livedo, often systemic.
Normal WBC does not exclude severe infection in immunocompromised patients.
Negative wound culture may occur after prior antibiotics – rely on clinical picture.
Gas on X‑ray can be absent early in necrotising fasciitis.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening pain, bullae, or skin necrosis.
Signs of sepsis: fever >38 °C, heart rate >100, respiratory rate >22, systolic BP <90 mmHg.
Loss of limb function or sensory loss.

faq.q: When should I admit a patient with cellulitis?
faq.a: Admit if there are systemic signs, comorbidities (diabetes, HIV), extensive disease, or if oral therapy is unreliable.

faq.q: Why add clindamycin for necrotising fasciitis?
faq.a: Clindamycin suppresses toxin production by streptococci and staphylococci, improving outcomes.

faq.q: Can I treat an abscess with antibiotics alone?
faq.a: No – drainage is essential; antibiotics alone rarely eradicate a collection.

exam: A 45‑year‑old diabetic presents with a painful, swollen foot and foul‑smelling discharge – what is your immediate management? — Recognise diabetic foot infection, obtain wound cultures if possible, start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram‑negatives and anaerobes, arrange surgical debridement.

A patient with a rapidly expanding erythematous thigh reports pain out of proportion – which red flag does this represent and what is the next step? — Pain disproportionate to exam suggests necrotising fasciitis; obtain urgent imaging if available, start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics, call for emergency surgical debridement.

You have a child with a bite wound from a dog, no tetanus immunisation history – what prophylaxis is required? — Give tetanus toxoid (or tetanus immunoglobulin if wound is dirty and immunisation unknown) and start amoxicillin‑clavulanate for Pasteurella coverage.

In a resource‑limited setting, blood cultures are unavailable – how do you decide on antibiotic choice for severe cellulitis? — Base choice on local epidemiology: cover MSSA with flucloxacillin; add clindamycin if MRSA prevalence is high or toxin‑mediated disease suspected.

A patient on chronic steroids develops a painless, indurated area with overlying erythema – what alternative diagnosis should you consider? — Consider fungal infection (e.g., sporotrichosis) or atypical mycobacterial infection; obtain tissue biopsy if possible.

Why is vancomycin avoided in a patient with severe renal impairment when treating MRSA SSTI? — Vancomycin is nephrotoxic; use linezolid or daptomycin if available, or adjust dose with careful monitoring.

What clinical feature distinguishes cellulitis from erythema nodosum? — Cellulitis has warmth, tenderness, and systemic signs; erythema nodosum presents as tender nodules without warmth or systemic infection.

A patient with necrotising fasciitis is haemodynamically unstable – what adjunctive therapy improves survival? — Early aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and immediate surgical debridement; consider IV immunoglobulin for streptococcal toxic shock.
